summary: Describes a mechanism to support the multicast needs of Layer 3 protocols over ATM networks, and applies it to IP multicasting. It addresses how a connection-oriented network can deliver one-to-many traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM links carry traffic between pairs of devices, so a sender cannot reach a whole group at once. This document adds a registry that tells senders who the group members are, plus rules for building the one-to-many connection that carries the traffic.

subtitle: How IP multicast gets a membership registry and a one-to-many circuit on a network that only connects callers in pairs.

tldr.problem: IP multicast assumes the link layer can send to an abstract group address, but ATM under UNI 3.0/3.1 offers only point to point and point to multipoint virtual circuits, where the sender must already know every receiver.
tldr.mechanism: A Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) keeps a registry that maps each layer 3 group address to the ATM addresses of its members. Endpoints ask it for the member list, build point to multipoint VCs either as a mesh of VCs or through an ATM level multicast server, and the MARS tells them about later joins and leaves.
tldr.outcome: Layer 3 protocols, IPv4 in particular, can multicast across an ATM cluster. Each group can use a VC mesh or a multicast server, and endpoints cannot tell which.

today: RFC 2022 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1996. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text itself leaves several matters, such as how backup MARSs coordinate with each other, for future documents.

sections.title: The Multicast Problem on ATM
sections.content:
Multicasting is the process whereby a source host or protocol entity sends a packet to several destinations at the same time using a single local transmit operation. Unicast and broadcast are special cases of it.

Most network layer models, such as the one in RFC 1112 for IP multicasting, assume that a source can send its packets to an abstract multicast group address and that the link layer will deliver them, as Ethernet does. Under IPv4 the group addresses are the range 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255. On Ethernet an algorithmic mapping turns a group address into an Ethernet multicast address, so no address resolution is needed before sending.

ATM does not offer that abstraction. The ATM Forum signalling specifications UNI 3.0 and UNI 3.1 support unicast with point to point, bidirectional VCs and multicast with point to multipoint, unidirectional VCs. The key limitation is that the sender must know each intended recipient in advance and set up a VC with itself as the root node and the recipients as leaf nodes. Only the root may add or remove leaves.

The RFC has two goals: a group address registration and membership distribution mechanism so that UNI 3.0/3.1 networks can support the multicast service of protocols such as IP, and specific endpoint behaviours for managing the point to multipoint VCs that carry the traffic. Quality of service is left out. VCs are requested with Unspecified Bit Rate (UBR) service by default, following the way the IETF uses VCs for unicast IP.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM links join two devices at a time. A sender that wants to reach twenty receivers must first learn who the twenty are, and this document supplies both the way to find out and the way to connect them.

sections.title: VC Meshes and Multicast Servers
sections.content:
The RFC describes two ways to deliver a multicast packet over ATM. In a VC mesh, each source sets up its own point to multipoint VC to the group members it has been told about. A host that both sends and receives ends up originating one VC and terminating one for every other active sender, and the criss-crossing of VCs across the network gives the name.

With a multicast server (MCS), each source opens a VC to the MCS. The server reassembles the incoming AAL_SDUs and queues them for transmission on its single outgoing point to multipoint VC. A side effect is that a sender which is also a member receives copies of its own packets back.

The trade-offs are spelled out. A mesh has no single congestion point, and it likely gives higher throughput and lower latency because there is no intermediate reassembly of AAL_SDUs. But its resource use is higher, since every group member's interface must terminate a VC per sender, while a multicast server needs only 2 VCs per member, one out and one in, no matter how many senders there are. Signalling load also differs: with a multicast server a membership change touches a single VC, while in a mesh signalling events happen at the signalling entities of every traffic source. Finally, the multicast server introduces the reflected packet problem, which needs extra information in each AAL_SDU so that a source can recognise its own packets coming back.

The MARS architecture lets an administrator pick either approach for each group.
sections.plainLanguage: A mesh builds a separate circuit from each sender to the group. A server sits in the middle and copies everything it receives out to one shared circuit.

sections.title: The MARS and Its Cluster
sections.content:
The Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) is an extended version of the ATM ARP server from RFC 1577. Where the ARP server keeps pairs of IP and ATM addresses, the MARS keeps mappings of a layer 3 address to a list of ATM addresses, and it can be configured with them or learn them dynamically. The MARS generally does not interpret the layer 3 address field.

Each MARS manages a cluster: the set of ATM interfaces that choose to use direct ATM connections to multicast to each other. In practice a cluster is the set of endpoints that register with the same MARS. Traffic between interfaces in different clusters passes through an inter-cluster device, which in the IP world is a multicast router. Network administrators MUST give each Logical IP Subnet (LIS) its own MARS, creating a one-to-one mapping between cluster and unicast LIS.

Two control VCs carry membership news. The ClusterControlVC is a point to multipoint VC from the MARS to all registered cluster members, and the ServerControlVC reaches all registered multicast servers. Between a client and the MARS there is also a transient point to point VC for queries, closed after an idle period with a suggested minimum of 1 minute and a recommended default of 20 minutes. A client is configured with the ATM address of its MARS.

The MARS does not take part in the actual multicasting of data packets. A single ATM node may run several logical MARSs, each with its own unique ATM address, and one instance of a MARS may not serve more than one cluster.
sections.plainLanguage: Each ATM site has one registry, and the devices configured to use it form a group of their own. The registry hands out membership changes on a circuit that reaches every member at once.

sections.title: MARS Control Messages
sections.content:
By default, MARS control messages MUST be LLC/SNAP encapsulated with the codepoints 0xAA-AA-03, 0x00-00-5E and 0x00-03. These differ from the ones used by ATMARP, so a MARS and an ARP server can share a VC. A message has four parts: a fixed header, mandatory fields that depend on the operation, variable length addresses, and optional supplementary TLVs. A null address is encoded with zero length and takes no space in the message.

The fixed header holds mar$afn (address family, 16 bits, the value 0x000F for MARS messages), mar$pro (protocol identification, 56 bits, such as 0x800 for IPv4), a reserved field of 24 bits, mar$chksum (checksum across the whole message, 16 bits), mar$extoff (extensions offset, 16 bits), mar$op (operation code, 16 bits) and the type and length of the source ATM number and subaddress, 8 bits each.

The checksum is the standard IP checksum over the whole message, and it may be left out by setting it to zero, because the AAL5 CRC already protects the message. The operation code is split into two octets: the first is the protocol version, where 0 means the MARS protocol defined in this document, and the second is the operation itself.

Supplementary parameters are TLV elements that start on the first 32 bit boundary after the addresses and end with a Null TLV. The top 2 bits of the type tell a receiver what to do with a type it does not recognise: skip it, drop the message silently, or drop the message and report an error. A conforming implementation only has to recognise the Null TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Every control message opens with the same small block of fields. It says which of several message types follows, and which layer 3 protocol the message is about.

sections.title: Sending to a Group
sections.content:
When a layer 3 packet is passed down for a group with no open outgoing VC, the endpoint sends a MARS_REQUEST (operation 1) with the group address as the target. The MARS answers with one or more MARS_MULTI messages (operation 2) listing the member ATM addresses, or with a MARS_NAK (operation 6) if there are none, in which case the packet MUST be discarded silently. Each MARS_MULTI carries an end-of-reply flag and a 15 bit sequence number, and the client discards the reply and asks again if it detects a jump in the sequence or a lost final part. A timer MUST flag the failure of the last part to arrive, with a recommended default of 10 seconds.

The RFC's example works out the size of a reply. With 4 byte protocol addresses, 20 byte ATM numbers and no subaddresses, a message carrying n members is 60 plus 20n bytes long, so with the default MTU of 9180 bytes a single MARS_MULTI can hold at most 456 member addresses.

The endpoint then issues L_MULTI_RQ for the first address and L_MULTI_ADD for each other one, sends the packet, and keeps the VC as the active path for that group. A failed add is retried after a random delay of 5 to 10 seconds, and the delay doubles on each failure. The VC may be considered up before the failed adds have been reissued, because waiting for every member would delay the first packet. Each VC MUST have a configurable inactivity timer, and when it expires an L_RELEASE is issued; the timer SHOULD be no less than 1 minute, and a default of 20 minutes is recommended.

Multicast data uses its own LLC/SNAP encapsulation so that a sender can detect reflected packets from a multicast server. Clients MUST transmit using Type #1, which carries the sender's 2 octet Cluster Member ID before the protocol type, and MUST accept Type #1 or Type #2. A receiver silently drops a Type #1 packet whose Cluster Member ID matches its own.
sections.plainLanguage: To send to a group, an endpoint asks the registry for the member list, sets up the circuit to those members, and puts the packet on it.

sections.title: Joining, Leaving and Registering
sections.content:
An endpoint first registers by sending a MARS_JOIN (operation 4) with the register flag set. The MARS adds it as a leaf of the ClusterControlVC and assigns a 16 bit Cluster Member ID (CMI). To join a group the endpoint sends a MARS_JOIN with a <min,max> address pair, and a MARS_LEAVE (operation 5) to leave. The MARS rebroadcasts these on the ClusterControlVC so that senders can add or drop leaves with L_MULTI_ADD and L_MULTI_DROP. The client resends a join or leave until it sees a copy come back, over an interval that should be no shorter than 5 seconds, with 10 seconds recommended, and the attempt is flagged as a failure after 5 retransmissions.

A pair can span a block of addresses, which lets a multicast router join the whole Class D space from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 or only part of it. Routers can also send a MARS_GROUPLIST_REQUEST (operation 10) and get a MARS_GROUPLIST_REPLY (operation 11) listing the groups that have layer 3 members. The RFC recommends this as a way of avoiding sending IGMP queries into the cluster.

A multicast server registers with MARS_MSERV (operation 3) and announces a group with it. For a group served by a multicast server, the MARS gives ordinary clients the server's address instead of the member list, and sends a MARS_MIGRATE (operation 13) to move existing senders from a mesh to the server. Members are passed to the server with MARS_SJOIN (operation 18) and MARS_SLEAVE (operation 19) on the ServerControlVC. Because there is no synchronisation protocol between multicast servers, an administrator MUST NOT allow more than one logical server for a group.

Endpoints may keep a table of alternative MARS addresses for use when the current one fails. After a failure the client waits a random 1 to 10 seconds, then re-registers and rejoins its groups, and if that fails it waits at least 1 minute before trying the next address. The MARS sends a MARS_REDIRECT_MAP (operation 12) on the ClusterControlVC at least every 2 minutes, with 1 minute recommended, carrying its list of backups. A hard redirect re-registers and rejoins groups, while a soft redirect only opens a VC to the new MARS and registers.
sections.plainLanguage: A device announces that it wants to receive a group, and keeps repeating the announcement until it sees its own message come back. The registry then tells the senders to add it.

sections.title: Staying in Sync with the Cluster Sequence Number
sections.content:
Members must not miss membership changes, so the MARS keeps a 32 bit Cluster Sequence Number that goes up by one for every transmission on the ClusterControlVC, whether or not that transmission carries a change. Each client keeps its own Host Sequence Number and compares the two. If the difference is not 0 or 1, the client has missed something and must revalidate. All these calculations MUST be done as unsigned 32 bit arithmetic.

Revalidation re-issues a MARS_REQUEST for each affected group and compares the returned member set with the set held locally. An L_MULTI_DROP is issued for a node that is no longer a member and an L_MULTI_ADD for one that has joined. Unlike the first time a VC is built, packet transmission continues on the open VC while it is revalidated, which keeps the disruption to running traffic small. Each open VC has a flag that is checked every time a packet is queued on it, and when an event demands revalidation the flag is set at a random time between 1 and 10 seconds, which staggers the revalidation requests.

Two other events lead to revalidation. When a leaf node drops itself, indicated by an ERR_L_DROP, its ATM address is removed from the set the endpoint holds and the flag is set after a random 1 to 10 seconds. When an ERR_L_RELEASE arrives, the whole set is cleared and the VC is treated as shut down, so the next packet to that group builds a new one.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message from the registry carries a counter. If the counter skips a value, the client knows it missed a change and asks for the member list again.

sections.title: Key Decisions and Open Issues
sections.content:
The RFC lists the decisions it makes. A MARS coordinates and distributes mappings from layer 3 group addresses to ATM endpoints. A cluster defines the scope of a MARS and the set of endpoints willing to take part in link level multicasting. A MARS supports either VC meshes or ATM level multicast servers. LLC/SNAP encapsulation of the control messages lets MARS and ATMARP traffic share VCs. A set of new message types carries the traffic: MARS_JOIN, MARS_LEAVE and MARS_REQUEST for membership, MARS_MULTI for the answer, MARS_MSERV and MARS_UNSERV for multicast servers, MARS_SJOIN and MARS_SLEAVE for passing changes to those servers, MARS_GROUPLIST_REQUEST and MARS_GROUPLIST_REPLY for listing groups with layer 3 members, MARS_REDIRECT_MAP for backup MARS addresses, and MARS_MIGRATE for moving a group from a mesh to a server.

Several questions are left open. There is no specification yet for how backup MARSs coordinate with each other, and the default is to have only one MARS per cluster. The same is true of several multicast servers for one group, and the default is one server per group. The MARS relies on a cluster member dropping off the ClusterControlVC to notice that it has died, and it is not clear whether more is needed to remove dead members. Layer 3 broadcast and layer 3 unicast are not discussed as special cases of multicasting. The future development of ATM Group Addresses and Leaf Initiated Join is not addressed, and the RFC notes that those developments would not fix the problems it has with VC scarcity. Possible changes to how the reserved header field and the address family field are read are left for further study.

The security considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not addressed in this document. The only trust check the text describes is for a soft redirect, where a cluster member must check that the node at the other end of the VC carrying the MARS_REDIRECT_MAP is the MARS it trusts.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets out no security rules. It does list the parts of the design that still need decisions, such as how two registries would hand over to each other.

viz.caption: THE FIXED HEADER OF A MARS CONTROL MESSAGE (SECTION 4.3)

items.title: mar$afn, 16 bits
items.text: Address family of the link layer addresses carried. The value 0x000F is used by MARS messages.

items.title: mar$pro, 56 bits
items.text: Protocol identification, such as IPv4, IPv6 or AppleTalk.

items.title: mar$chksum, 16 bits
items.text: Checksum across the whole message. It may be set to zero because the AAL5 CRC already protects the message.

items.title: mar$extoff, 16 bits
items.text: Offset to the optional list of supplementary TLVs. Zero means there are none.

items.title: mar$op, 16 bits
items.text: Operation code, split into a version octet and a type octet.

items.title: mar$shtl and mar$sstl, 8 bits each
items.text: Type and length of the source ATM number and of the source ATM subaddress.

items.label: MARS_REQUEST
items.desc: Ask the MARS for the members of a group.

items.label: MARS_MULTI
items.desc: Returns the ATM addresses of the group members.

items.label: MARS_MSERV
items.desc: A multicast server registers, or offers to serve a group.

items.label: MARS_JOIN
items.desc: Register with the MARS, or join a group.

items.label: MARS_LEAVE
items.desc: Deregister from the MARS, or leave a group.

items.label: MARS_NAK
items.desc: No mapping was found, so the group is empty.

items.label: MARS_UNSERV
items.desc: A multicast server stops serving a group.

items.label: MARS_SJOIN
items.desc: A join passed on to the multicast servers.

items.label: MARS_SLEAVE
items.desc: A leave passed on to the multicast servers.

items.label: MARS_GROUPLIST_REQUEST
items.desc: Ask which groups have layer 3 members.

items.label: MARS_GROUPLIST_REPLY
items.desc: The list of groups that have layer 3 members.

items.label: MARS_REDIRECT_MAP
items.desc: The list of backup MARS addresses. It can also force a move.

items.label: MARS_MIGRATE
items.desc: Moves senders from a VC mesh to a multicast server.
